rem:hecke-blitvic-pair-partition-mechani: Remark Why the Markov-trace moments are not a pair-partition sum. Blitvić's theorem applies when joint moments of centred variables vanish in odd degree and decompose as a sum over pair-partitions in even degree. For the Hecke generators under the Markov trace the first condition already fails: the third centred moment of a single generator is non-zero (the Blitvić-hypothesis proposition). The quadratic relation reduces a repeated generator to a combination of 1 and \sigma_i, not to a pairing, so the Markov-trace moments are not a pair-partition sum.
prf:hecke-satisfies-blitvic-hypothesis:
Proof Proof: the third centred moment of a Hecke generator. Write X for a polynomial variable and p(X) = X^{2} - hX - 1. The quadratic relation \sigma^{2} = h\sigma + 1 says p(\sigma) = 0, so any polynomial in \sigma can be reduced modulo p before the trace is taken. By linearity, \mathrm{tr}(aX + b)|_{X=\sigma} = a z + b.

Variance. In K[X],

  (X - z)^{2} = p(X) + (h - 2z)\,X + (1 + z^{2}),

so \mathrm{tr}(\tilde\sigma^{2}) = (h - 2z)z + 1 + z^{2} = hz + 1 - z^{2}.

Third moment. In K[X],

  (X - z)^{3} = (X + h - 3z)\,p(X) + \bigl(h^{2} + 1 - 3hz + 3z^{2}\bigr)X + \bigl(h - 3z - z^{3}\bigr),

so

  \mathrm{tr}(\tilde\sigma^{3}) = (h^{2} + 1 - 3hz + 3z^{2})\,z + h - 3z - z^{3}
  = (h^{2}+1)z + h - 3hz^{2} - 3z + 2z^{3}.

A Markov trace restricts to such a trace. For a Markov trace family on the Hecke tower, \mathrm{tr}_1 is K-linear with \mathrm{tr}_1(1) = 1, and the Markov property at x = 1 gives \mathrm{tr}_1(\sigma_0) = z.

The value at q = 2. Here h = 3/2 and z = 8/5, so

  \mathrm{tr}(\tilde\sigma^{3}) = \tfrac{13}{4}\cdot\tfrac{8}{5} + \tfrac{3}{2} - 3\cdot\tfrac{3}{2}\cdot\tfrac{64}{25} - \tfrac{24}{5} + 2\cdot\tfrac{512}{125} = -\tfrac{357}{250}.

Blitvić's hypothesis requires every odd centred moment to vanish, so it fails. \square

Where the earlier argument went wrong. It applied the Markov property to a factor \tilde\sigma_i inside a word in which the same index i occurs again. The Markov property \mathrm{tr}(x\sigma_n) = z\,\mathrm{tr}(x) holds only for x \in H_n(q), that is, when \sigma_n does not occur in x. It does not apply when the index is repeated.
rem:hecke-satisfies-blitvic-hypothesis-i: Remark Why the odd moments do not vanish. The obstruction comes from the quadratic relation. A repeated generator does not reduce to the identity: \sigma^{2} = h\sigma + 1 leaves a term in \sigma itself, and a non-zero linear term survives in every power. A (q,t)-Gaussian has a symmetric moment sequence. The centred Hecke generator has eigenvalues q - z and -q^{-1} - z, which are not negatives of each other, so its distribution under \mathrm{tr} is not symmetric.
rem:sniady-genus-grading-dimension-obstr:
Remark Genus grading of character observables and the non-polynomiality of hook dimensions. At the classical specialisation q = 1, where H_k(1) \cong \mathbb{C}[S_k], the non-vanishing third moment of the Blitvić-hypothesis proposition has its symmetric-group counterpart in the three-cycle character observable on Young diagrams \lambda \vdash k. Let \mathcal{A} denote the Kerov--Olshanski algebra of polynomial functions on Young diagrams, generated by the normalised conjugacy-class indicators \Sigma_{k_1, \dots, k_t} (or equivalently by the transition-measure free cumulants R_2, R_3, R_4, \dots). For any set partition \pi of an n-element set, Piotr Śniady proves that the partition-indexed indicator \Sigma_\pi \in \mathcal{A} has filtration degree

  \deg \Sigma_\pi = n - 2\,\mathrm{genus}_\pi

[sniady2006asymptotics, §3.1, Prop. 3.4], so non-crossing partitions (\mathrm{genus}_\pi = 0) govern the leading order and evercrossing partitions of genus 1 govern the first subleading correction to normalised characters and Jucys--Murphy free cumulants [sniady2006asymptotics, §4.5, Thms. 4.13--4.14]. In particular, the normalised three-cycle central character

  \omega_3(\lambda) = \frac{k(k-1)(k-2)\,\chi^\lambda((123))}{3\,f^\lambda} = \sum_{\square \in \lambda} c(\square)^2 - \binom{k}{2}

and the fourth free cumulant R_4(\lambda) = 3\,\omega_3(\lambda) - k both belong to \mathcal{A} in filtration degree 4, and under the Plancherel measure \mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{Planch}}(\lambda) = (f^\lambda)^2 / k! their expectations satisfy \mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{Planch}}[\omega_3] = 0 and \mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{Planch}}[R_4] = -k.

By contrast, the dimension-cubed three-cycle sum

  \sum_{\lambda \vdash k} (f^\lambda)^3\,\omega_3(\lambda)
  = \frac{k(k-1)(k-2)}{3} \sum_{\lambda \vdash k} (f^\lambda)^2\,\chi^\lambda((123))
  = k!\,\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathrm{Planch}}\bigl(f^\lambda,\, \omega_3(\lambda)\bigr)
  = \frac{k!}{3}\,\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathrm{Planch}}\bigl(f^\lambda,\, R_4(\lambda)\bigr)

weights \omega_3 \in \mathcal{A} by an additional factor of the hook-length dimension f^\lambda = k! / \prod_{\square \in \lambda} h(\square). Because f^\lambda grows on the scale \sqrt{k!} across typical Plancherel shapes rather than polynomially in the free cumulants (R_m)_{m \ge 2}, neither f^\lambda nor \ln f^\lambda lies in \mathcal{A}. Proposition~3.4 of [sniady2006asymptotics] grades Plancherel joint cumulants of elements within \mathcal{A}, so the genus filtration controls the \omega_3 factor in \mathrm{Cov}_{\mathrm{Planch}}(f^\lambda, R_4) without assigning a finite filtration degree or leading genus term to the product f^\lambda\,\omega_3(\lambda). Bounding the sign of \mathrm{Cov}_{\mathrm{Planch}}(f^\lambda, R_4) therefore requires a direct functional representation of f^\lambda or \ln f^\lambda over Young diagrams rather than finite-genus character asymptotics inside \mathcal{A}.
def:bar-involution:
Definition Bar-involution and its P_{\mathrm{avg}} / P_{\mathrm{skew}} projections: the canonical q \leftrightarrow q^{-1}, \sigma \leftrightarrow \sigma^{-1} involution on the Hecke algebra, splitting every H_n(q)-quantity into a bar-symmetric (even/cosh/cos/\mathrm{Li}_2^q-like) part the framework retains and a bar-anti-symmetric (odd/sinh/sin/\Phi_q-like) part the framework projects away. The bar-involution \overline{(\cdot)} \colon H_n(q) \to H_n(q) is the ring anti-involution on the Iwahori–Hecke algebra defined by:

\overline{\sigma_i} \;=\; \sigma_i^{-1}, \qquad \overline{q} \;=\; q^{-1}.
rem:bar-involution-properties:
Remark Bar-involution: the P_{\mathrm{avg}} / P_{\mathrm{skew}} canonical projections and the QOU bar-type classification. The bar-involution satisfies \overline{\overline x} = x. Over a field of characteristic \ne 2, every x \in H_n(q) decomposes uniquely into a bar-symmetric (even) part P_{\mathrm{avg}}(x) and a bar-anti-symmetric (odd) part P_{\mathrm{skew}}(x).

The framework asserts that P_{\mathrm{avg}} is the canonical projection: the bar-symmetric part represents physical observables, while the bar-anti-symmetric part is projected away. This applies systematically across operations, retaining functions like \cos and \cosh while discarding \sin and \sinh.

Geometrically, the bar-involution corresponds to reflecting the braid diagram, swapping positive and negative crossings.
rem:bar-involution-c5-algebraic-identiti:
Remark Bar-symmetric algebraic identities: half-step factorization of h, Hoefsmit-Quantum-2 (b^2 = 1 - 1/[2]_q^2), and the c_5 closed form. The parameter h = q - q^{-1} factors into h_{1/2} = q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2} and q^{1/2} + q^{-1/2}. The bar-anti-symmetry of h stems entirely from h_{1/2}; the second factor is bar-invariant.

The second factor is not 1/z. For the Markov parameter z = q^3/(q^2+1), its reciprocal is 1/z = (q^2+1)/q^3 = [2]_q/q^2 = 1.632151991505175166202 at q_0, whereas q^{1/2} + q^{-1/2} = 2.0027\ldots is a Temperley–Lieb loop expression at the half-argument q^{1/2}, not the reciprocal of the Hecke generator's Markov trace. Moreover, 1/[2]_q^2, the bar-even quantity from which the c_5 closed form below is built, equals the two-row Markov weight y_{(2,1)} — the isospin-singlet weight \mu_-.

The Hoefsmit-Quantum-2 identity is b^2(q) = 1 - 1/[2]_q^2. From this, the c_5 closed form follows:

c_5(q) \;=\; -\tfrac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{[2]_q^2} \;=\; -\tfrac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{h^2 + 4}.

Both terms are strictly even functions of h. The constant -3/2 corresponds to half the dimension of the non-sign Wedderburn blocks of the symmetric group S_3. This identifies the -1/2 fingerprint in the empirical decomposition as the bar-symmetric contribution from the non-sign sector at the classical limit.

Testing the sequence c_k(q) reveals that the c_5 outlier only appears at the silver ratio, not at the golden ratio, confirming it is an inert-prime fingerprint tied to the \beta-decay null.
rem:bar-involution-geometric-kac-sunada:
Remark Geometric and Kac–Sunada readings of the bar-involution. The bar-involution projection corresponds to orientation-averaging geometrically. It yields averaged crossings for knots, unsigned winding for color tubes, symmetrized Wilson loops on the exceptional divisor, and the contact volume form \alpha \wedge d\alpha.

The Kac-Sunada theorem establishes that distinct manifolds can be isospectral. Similarly, distinct braids can share the same Hecke trace \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta) at fixed q. However, requiring the trace to match at both q and q^{-1} imposes a much tighter constraint. The physical theory must hear the bar-symmetrized spectrum, forcing the use of the bar-symmetric projection.

Two different objects called "Fricke" (literature). The name is attached in this corpus to two unrelated things. The Fricke trace relation invoked in the mass-theory blocks is a relation among traces of matrices, used to fix a knot's chirality factor. The Fricke involution is the map \tau \mapsto -1/(N\tau) on the upper half-plane, which normalises \Gamma_0(N) and extends to the Atkin–Lehner involutions; it is the object proposed as a candidate partner of the bar-involution in the \tau-dictionary audits, where every natural candidate tested so far fails the gate set there. In string compactifications the same map, acting on the axio-dilaton as S \mapsto -1/(NS), is called Fricke S-duality, and a model is self-dual under it exactly when its electric–magnetic charge lattice is N-modular, that is, isometric to its dual lattice rescaled by N [arxiv-1504.07260v3, §1.1]. That lattice characterisation is a statement about the involution, not about the trace relation, and nothing in this block identifies the bar-involution with either.
rem:bar-involution-grading-lean-proofs:
Remark The \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} bar-grading: Lean \leftrightarrow paper proof bridge. This remark records the \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} bar-grading induced by the bar-involution: the bar-grading subring/module structure, with proofs.

Proofs

The results split into three sections by structural prerequisite.

Bar-grading over a commutative ring R

Proposition. x = P_{\mathrm{avg}}(x) + P_{\mathrm{skew}}(x). Proof. \frac{x + \overline x}{2} + \frac{x - \overline x}{2} = \frac{2x}{2} = x. \square

Proposition. 0 and 1 are bar-symmetric. Proof. Direct from \overline 0 = 0 and \overline 1 = 1. \square

Proposition. Sum of bar-symmetric is bar-symmetric. Proof. \overline{x+y} = \overline x + \overline y = x + y. \square

Proposition. Product of bar-symmetric is bar-symmetric. Proof. \overline{x \cdot y} = \overline x \cdot \overline y = x \cdot y. \square

Proposition. Sum of bar-anti-symmetric is bar-anti-symmetric. Proof. \overline{x+y} = \overline x + \overline y = -x + (-y) = -(x+y). \square

Theorem. x, y bar-anti-symmetric \Rightarrow x \cdot y bar-symmetric. Proof. \overline{x \cdot y} = \overline x \cdot \overline y = (-x)(-y) = x \cdot y. This is the "anti \times anti = sym" identity that generates the bar-symmetric content from bar-anti-symmetric kernels (e.g., h^2 bar-sym from h bar-anti-sym). \square

Theorem. x bar-symmetric, y bar-anti-symmetric \Rightarrow x \cdot y bar-anti-symmetric. Proof. \overline{x \cdot y} = \overline x \cdot \overline y = x \cdot (-y) = -(x \cdot y). \square

Proposition. \overline{-x} = -\overline x — bar commutes with negation. Proof. From x + (-x) = 0 and bar additive: \overline x + \overline{-x} = \overline 0 = 0, hence \overline{-x} = -\overline x. \square

Proposition. Negation preserves both grading sectors. Proof. For sym: \overline{-x} = -\overline x = -x. For anti-sym: \overline{-x} = -\overline x = -(-x) = x = -(-x). \square

Theorem. x bar-anti-sym \Rightarrow x^{2n} bar-symmetric. Proof. Induction on n. Base (n=0): x^0 = 1 bar-symmetric. Step: x^{2(k+1)} = x^{2k} \cdot (x \cdot x); x^{2k} bar-sym by IH, x \cdot x bar-sym by the anti \times anti theorem above; product bar-sym by closure under products. \square

Theorem. x bar-anti-sym \Rightarrow x^{2n+1} bar-anti-symmetric. Proof. x^{2n+1} = x^{2n} \cdot x; x^{2n} bar-sym (above), x bar-anti-sym (hypothesis); product bar-anti-sym by the sym \times anti theorem above. \square

Bar on integer scalars

Proposition. \overline 2 = 2. Proof. \overline 2 = \overline{1 + 1} = \overline 1 + \overline 1 = 1 + 1 = 2. \square

Proposition. \overline n = n for every n \in \mathbb{N}. Proof. Induction on n. Base: \overline 0 = 0. Step: \overline{k+1} = \overline k + \overline 1 = k + 1. \square

Proposition. Every natural-number scalar is bar-symmetric. Proof. Restatement of \overline n = n (above) as bar-symmetry. \square

Projection theorems (require R to be a field)

Proposition. \overline{x^{-1}} = (\overline x)^{-1} over a field. Proof. If x = 0: both sides are 0 (from \overline 0 = 0 + 0^{-1} = 0 convention). If x \neq 0: \overline x \neq 0 (bar is injective by involutivity), and \overline x \cdot \overline{x^{-1}} = \overline{x \cdot x^{-1}} = \overline 1 = 1, hence \overline{x^{-1}} = (\overline x)^{-1}. \square

Proposition. \overline{1/2} = 1/2 over a field. Proof. \overline{1/2} = \overline{1 \cdot 2^{-1}} = \overline 1 \cdot (\overline 2)^{-1} = 1 \cdot 2^{-1} = 1/2, using \overline{x^{-1}} = (\overline x)^{-1} and \overline 2 = 2. \square

Proposition. Every integer scalar is bar-symmetric. Proof. For n = \mathrm{ofNat}\, k: use \overline k = k. For n = \mathrm{negSucc}\, k = -(k+1): \overline{-(k+1)} = -\overline{k+1} = -(k+1), since bar commutes with negation and fixes natural-number scalars. \square

Proposition. If x is bar-symmetric, P_{\mathrm{avg}}(x) = x. Proof. P_{\mathrm{avg}}(x) = (x + \overline x)/2 = (x + x)/2 = x. \square

Proposition. If x is bar-anti-symmetric, P_{\mathrm{avg}}(x) = 0. Proof. P_{\mathrm{avg}}(x) = (x + \overline x)/2 = (x - x)/2 = 0. \square

Proposition. If x is bar-anti-symmetric, P_{\mathrm{skew}}(x) = x. Proof. P_{\mathrm{skew}}(x) = (x - \overline x)/2 = (x - (-x))/2 = x. \square

Proposition. If x is bar-symmetric, P_{\mathrm{skew}}(x) = 0. Proof. P_{\mathrm{skew}}(x) = (x - \overline x)/2 = (x - x)/2 = 0. \square

Theorem. For bar-anti-sym x: P_{\mathrm{avg}}(x^{2n}) = x^{2n}. Proof. x^{2n} is bar-symmetric (above); apply the bar-symmetric case of P_{\mathrm{avg}}. \square

Theorem. For bar-anti-sym x: P_{\mathrm{avg}}(x^{2n+1}) = 0. Proof. x^{2n+1} is bar-anti-sym (above); apply the bar-anti-symmetric case of P_{\mathrm{avg}}. This is "the framework projects away odd-power components" at the formal level. \square

Theorem. P_{\mathrm{avg}}(x) is bar-symmetric for every x. Proof. \overline{P_{\mathrm{avg}}(x)} = \overline{(x + \overline x)/2} = \overline{x + \overline x} \cdot \overline{1/2} = (\overline x + x) \cdot (1/2) = P_{\mathrm{avg}}(x), using \overline{1/2} = 1/2. \square

Theorem. P_{\mathrm{avg}}^2 = P_{\mathrm{avg}}. Proof. P_{\mathrm{avg}}(x) is bar-symmetric by the previous theorem; applying P_{\mathrm{avg}} to a bar-symmetric input gives the input back (bar-symmetric case above). \square

Theorem. P_{\mathrm{skew}}(x) is bar-anti-symmetric. Proof. \overline{P_{\mathrm{skew}}(x)} = \overline{(x - \overline x)/2} = (\overline x - x) \cdot (1/2) = -P_{\mathrm{skew}}(x). \square

Theorem. P_{\mathrm{skew}}^2 = P_{\mathrm{skew}}. Proof. Analogous to P_{\mathrm{avg}} idempotency, using P_{\mathrm{skew}}(x) = x for bar-anti-symmetric x. \square
rem:braid-group-n-strand: Remark n-strand braid group, Markov closure, and Hecke quadratic quotient: axiomatic framework generalising the 2-strand \mathbf{B}_2 foundation and 3-strand typed-\mathbf{B}_3 infrastructure. To compute the \mathrm{tr}_M(K_1 \sqcup K_2) inter-knot decoupling, the B_3 framework generalises to arbitrary n-strand braid groups and Hecke quotients. Results stated for general n then specialise to each fixed n as higher strand numbers are analysed.
rem:h3-hecke-idempotents:
Remark H_3(q) Hecke idempotents — explicit q-dimensions and per-block \sigma_i eigenvalues for the three Wedderburn blocks V_{(3)}, V_{(2,1)}, V_{(1^3)}, substantively backing \mathtt{QYoungSymmetrizers}\ 3\ q. The algebra H_3(q) contains three irreducible Wedderburn blocks. The symmetric block V_{(3)} and antisymmetric block V_{(1,1,1)} both have dimension 1. The mixed-symmetry block V_{(2,1)} has dimension [2]_q = q + q^{-1}. The sum of dimensions correctly recovers q + q^{-1} + 2.

The explicit projector normalization utilizes the S_3 Poincaré polynomial P(q) = 1 + 2q^2 + 2q^4 + q^6. Because P(q) \geq 1 > 0 for all real q, idempotency requires no genericity hypothesis beyond q \neq 0.
prop:coxeter-strong-exchange:
Proposition Strong exchange for Coxeter systems, via the reflection cocycle. Let (W, S) be a Coxeter system with length function \ell, let \omega = (s_{i_1}, \dots, s_{i_k}) be any word in the generators (not necessarily reduced), and let t be a reflection of W with \ell(\pi(\omega)\, t) < \ell(\pi(\omega)), where \pi(\omega) denotes the product of the word. Then some single letter of \omega can be deleted: there is an index j < k with

\pi(\omega)\, t \;=\; \pi(\omega \setminus j),

where \omega \setminus j is the word with its j-th letter erased.

The proof is the classical reflection-cocycle construction. Each generator s acts on W \times \mathbb{Z}/2 by (w, \varepsilon) \mapsto (s w s,\; \varepsilon + [w = s]); these involutions satisfy the Coxeter relations because the inversion sequence of the doubled braid word consists of two identical halves, so every \mathbb{Z}/2 parity count cancels. The resulting homomorphism W \to \mathrm{Perm}(W \times \mathbb{Z}/2) makes the parity \eta(w, t) of the number of occurrences of t in the right inversion sequence independent of the chosen word for w. The cocycle law gives \eta(t, t) = 1 for every reflection, hence \eta(wt, t) = 1 + \eta(w, t), and a length descent forces \eta(w, t) = 1; a positive parity locates an occurrence of t in the inversion sequence, and deleting that letter realises the product. No induction on length and no reduced-word hypothesis is needed.
prop:coxeter-parabolic-transversal:
Proposition Parabolic transversals and the Hecke presentation laws at every rank. Let (W, S) be a Coxeter system and s_i, s_j a generator pair with m_{ij} = 3 (respectively m_{ij} = 2), and suppose the single word s_i s_j s_i (respectively s_i s_j) is reduced. Then:

  1. the standard parabolic subgroup W_{\{i,j\}} consists of exactly the six elements e, s_i, s_j, s_j s_i, s_i s_j, s_i s_j s_i (respectively the four elements e, s_i, s_j, s_i s_j);
  2. every left coset of W_{\{i,j\}} has a unique minimal-length representative, and the factorization W \;\cong\; C \times W_{\{i,j\}} (minimal representatives times cell) is a bijection with additive lengths, \ell(u \cdot x) = \ell(u) + \ell(x);
  3. on the length-rule module W \to R over any commutative ring, the right-multiplication actions of s_i and s_j satisfy the braid relation (respectively far commutation).

The length additivity is the Bourbaki lifting lemma, obtained unconditionally from the strong exchange property; the coset datum localises each presentation law to a finite cell check. The single reducedness hypothesis per pair is the faithfulness of the dihedral cell — a theorem of Coxeter theory via the geometric representation, which is verified outright for the type-A_3 system by the permutation representation on four letters, so at that rung the braid and far-commutation laws hold with no hypothesis at all. Together with the quadratic relation, which holds outright at every rank, all three defining relation kinds of the Hecke algebra H_n(q) acting on its normal-form basis flow from the Coxeter-system data.
prop:coxeter-tits-residue-collapse:
Proposition The Tits residue collapsed: cell faithfulness is simple-distinctness. Let (W, S) be a Coxeter system and s_i, s_j a generator pair with m_{ij} = 3 (respectively m_{ij} = 2). Then

[s_i, s_j, s_i] \text{ is reduced}
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
s_i \neq s_j

(respectively [s_i, s_j] is reduced \Leftrightarrow s_i \neq s_j).

The forward direction is elementary. For the converse the reflection cocycle is used quantitatively: pairwise-distinct reflections t with cocycle value \eta(w, t) = 1 bound the length of w from below, because each such reflection occurs in the inversion sequence of any reduced word for w. The inversion sequence of the cell word is computed in closed form — [\,s_j,\; s_i s_j s_i,\; s_i\,] at m_{ij} = 3, the first entry collapsing by the braid relation, and [\,s_i,\; s_j\,] at m_{ij} = 2 — and simple-distinctness makes its entries pairwise distinct, forcing \ell \geq the word length.

Consequently the parabolic transversals, and with them the braid and far-commutation relations on the length-rule module, require only s_i \neq s_j per pair: nothing about lengths or words survives in the residue. What remains of Tits faithfulness, per generator pair, is exactly injectivity of the simple-reflection map — the point where the geometric representation classically enters.
prop:coxeter-geometric-representation:
Proposition The geometric representation: simple-injectivity at every Coxeter system. Let M be a Coxeter matrix over an index set B. On the free module \bigoplus_{i \in B} \mathbb{R}\,\alpha_i equip the pairing with matrix entries \langle \alpha_i, \alpha_j \rangle = -\cos(\pi/m_{ij}) for i \neq j and \langle \alpha_i, \alpha_i \rangle = 1, and set

f_i \;=\; \mathrm{id} \;-\; 2\,\langle \alpha_i, \cdot\, \rangle\,
\alpha_i .

Then the f_i satisfy the Coxeter relations of M — (f_i f_j)^{m_{ij}} = 1 for every pair, at every bond order — so they assemble into the geometric representation of any Coxeter system (W, S) over M. Since f_i and f_j act with opposite signs on \alpha_i when i \neq j, the simple reflections of every Coxeter system are pairwise distinct: s_i \neq s_j with no hypothesis.

The bond-order relation at m_{ij} \geq 3 is a Chebyshev argument. Writing g = f_i f_j and tracking the scalar pair \bigl(\langle \alpha_i, g^k w \rangle, \langle \alpha_j, g^k w \rangle\bigr) of an arbitrary vector w, both components satisfy the second-order recursion

u_{k+2} \;=\; 2\cos\varphi \cdot u_{k+1} \;-\; u_k,
\qquad \varphi = \tfrac{2\pi}{m_{ij}},

whose solutions are trigonometric and hence m_{ij}-periodic. The action of g^k differs from the identity by singles accumulated from these scalars; periodicity and telescoping force both accumulated sums to vanish, the coefficient matrix being invertible because \cos^2(\pi/m_{ij}) < 1. Thus g^{m_{ij}} w = w. The remaining orders are elementary: m_{ij} = 2 is direct commutation of the two reflections, and the diagonal is the involution f_i^2 = 1.

Combined with the collapsed Tits residue, every hypothesis in the parabolic-transversal chain is discharged: the braid and far-commutation relations on the length-rule module hold for every Coxeter system unconditionally.
prop:tau-assignment-tower-square:
Proposition The \tau-assignment tower square: H_3 \hookrightarrow H_4 compatibility. Let \iota_{34} denote the inclusion of the H_3 normal-form module into the H_4 normal-form module by extension with zero, the 24-element basis being ordered with the H_3 basis as its prefix. At the monodromy point q = i write N_n = \sigma - i for the Jordan nilpotent of the generator action on the rank-n module. Then the tower data commute at every level:

  1. action: \iota_{34} intertwines the generator actions on the two modules;
  2. nilpotent: \iota_{34} \circ N_3 = N_4 \circ \iota_{34};
  3. trace: the rank-4 Markov trace restricts along \iota_{34} to the rank-3 Markov trace;
  4. assignment: the rank-4 \tau-assignment onto the genus-4 H^{1,0} model restricts along \iota_{34} to the rank-3 assignment, and likewise for the conjugate H^{0,1} partner;
  5. surjectivity: the image of either assignment is the full three-dimensional isotypic slot of H^{1,0}, with witnesses at rank 4 obtained by pushing rank-3 witnesses forward along \iota_{34}.

Moreover the square itself is not special to these two rungs. For any Coxeter system and any generator subset J, extension by zero along the parabolic coset decomposition intertwines both the generator actions and the q = i nilpotents, with no hypothesis beyond subgroup membership; and for any marked pair s_i, s_j with m_{ij} = 3 and s_i \neq s_j, an assignment with all four laws exists on the full group at every rank and on every parabolic containing the pair, factoring through the base-rung assignment by restriction to the six-element cell, with the corresponding restriction square commuting. Kernel exactness — the identification of the semisimple quotient with the isotypic slot — holds at the base rung n = 3; at higher rungs the assignment factors through a larger semisimple quotient without being injective on it. Strict pair-independence fails: at the A_3 rung the assignments for the two braid pairs are provably different functions, the indicator state of the longest cell element of one pair being read into the isotypic slot by that pair's assignment and annihilated by the other's. Coherence between distinct pairs holds along two proved edge classes: any symmetry of the Coxeter matrix, and any conjugation carrying one marked pair onto another, each inducing a group endomorphism along which the target pair's assignment is the pullback of the source pair's. The pair swap (s_i, s_j) \mapsto (s_j, s_i) is the proved exception: it transports the six-element cell by an index involution, but no map on the isotypic target — linear or otherwise — completes its square. The coherent edges assemble: on the category of marked pairs, with morphisms the group homomorphisms carrying one marking to the other, the assignment family is a natural transformation from the contravariant state functor to the constant isotypic functor, and both proved edge classes are isomorphisms, so the transformation restricts to the core groupoid of marked pairs. This is the correct sense in which the pair-dependent family is canonical: not a single pair-independent map — that is refuted — but a coherently indexed one. The two coherence directions compose — a groupoid edge between pairs inside a common parabolic pastes with the restriction square — and the Markov trace of the cell restriction is intertwined by every edge, so trace values are well-defined on marked-pair orbits and may be quoted without naming the pair.
rem:braid-link-types:
Remark Two-strand braid closure \widehat{\sigma^2} as the Hopf link with classical Jones value -2. Braids and links are treated here as explicit combinatorial objects. For 2-strand braids, the closure of \sigma_1^2 explicitly yields the Hopf link. This evaluates to the classical Jones value -2.

The 3-strand generalisation requires extracting the dominant 2-strand sub-braid at order \varepsilon^6. The reduction of this sub-braid closes to the Hopf link, yielding the same c_3 = -2 value. This identifies the perturbative mass coefficients mechanically from the topological scaffolding.
rem:markov-trace-inductive-limit:
Remark Markov trace on the inductive limit \mathbf{B}_\infty = \bigcup_n \mathbf{B}_n — single global trace operator \mathrm{tr}_M : \mathbf{B}_\infty \to \mathbb{R} deriving every per-n \mathtt{MarkovTraceN}\ n\ q via Jones-Wenzl axioms M1-M3 (M4 derived via the Hecke quadratic relation) on the inductive structure. The Markov trace extends to a single operator on the inductive limit of braid groups \mathbf{B}_\infty = \bigcup_n \mathbf{B}_n. The restrictions \mathrm{tr}_M\big|_{\mathbf{B}_n} yield the per-n trace. The inclusion \iota_n : \mathbf{B}_n \hookrightarrow \mathbf{B}_{n+1} adjoins a non-interacting strand on the right.

The existence of this global trace is taken as a single hypothesis, from which every per-n trace is derived by restriction, so no separate per-n assumption is needed. This treatment lies on the archimedean side of the algebraic→archimedean wall: it substitutes the aether parameter q_0 and uses real-analytic bounds, while the generic categorical identities remain valid over an abstract coefficient ring.
rem:affine-hecke-homology-prior-art:
Remark Prior art: Hochschild homology of affine Hecke algebras is independent of q. Let \mathcal{R} be a based root datum with finite Weyl group W, let T = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(X, \mathbb{C}^\times), and let \mathcal{H}(\mathcal{R}, q) be the associated affine Hecke algebra with positive, possibly unequal, parameters q. Maarten Solleveld [solleveld2022, Theorem 1(d), p. 3] (originally published in [solleveld2013]) constructs families of representations \pi(w, i, t, \epsilon) of \mathcal{H}(\mathcal{R}, q^\epsilon) and proves that, for \epsilon \notin \sqrt{-1}\,\mathbb{R}^\times, two of them have the same trace if and only if they share (w, i) and their torus parameters t lie in one Z_W(w)-orbit. For the same \epsilon the Hochschild homology is

HH_*\big(\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{R}, q^\epsilon)\big) \cong \bigoplus_{w \in \langle W \rangle}\bigoplus_{i=1}^{c(w)} \Omega^*(T_i^w)^{Z_W(w)} \cong \Omega^*(\widetilde{T})^W,

the W-invariant algebraic differential forms on the extended quotient \widetilde{T}/W; only the action of the centre Z(\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{R}, q^\epsilon)) \cong \mathcal{O}(T)^W shifts with q^\epsilon [solleveld2022, Theorem 2, pp. 3–4; §3.2]. A 2021 gap in the representation-family construction and its repair are discussed on pages 16, 18, 19 and 22 of [solleveld2022, Abstract].

In degree zero, HH_0\big(\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{R}, q^\epsilon)\big) \cong \mathcal{O}(\widetilde{T})^W is the cocentre \mathcal{H}/[\mathcal{H}, \mathcal{H}], whose linear dual classifies all trace functionals on \mathcal{H}(\mathcal{R}, q^\epsilon). Because \mathcal{O}(\widetilde{T})^W does not move with q^\epsilon, any q-dependence of an affine Hecke trace value arises from the choice of functional or representation evaluation rather than from deformation of the cocentre.

This affine trace space contrasts sharply with the finite Iwahori–Hecke subalgebras H_n(q) \subset \mathcal{H}(A_{n-1}, q) at generic q: H_n(q) is finite-dimensional semisimple, so \dim HH_0(H_n(q)) = p(n) is finite and spanned by the irreducible characters \chi_\lambda (\lambda \vdash n) rather than by continuous torus algebras \mathcal{O}(T_i^w)^{Z_W(w)}. On the two-strand per-pair electromagnetic channel H_2(q), \dim HH_0(H_2(q)) = 2 (spanned by \chi_{(2)} and \chi_{(1^2)}), while across the strand-adding tower H_n(q) \hookrightarrow H_{n+1}(q) the Markov stabilisation condition \mathrm{tr}_M(x\,\sigma_n^{\pm 1}) = z\,\mathrm{tr}_M(x) cuts out a unique normalised one-parameter trace family. Moreover, the inductive-limit trace on H_\infty(q) = \bigcup_n H_n(q) is not covered directly by Solleveld's theorem: H_\infty(q) is an increasing union across rank n - 1 \to \infty rather than the affine Hecke algebra of a fixed finite-rank root datum \mathcal{R}, so passing to the limit requires an independent argument.
prop:trm-hopf-sigma1-sq-closed-form:
Proposition Closed form for the canonical Markov trace of \sigma_1^2 (positive Hopf braid). The canonical Markov trace of \sigma_1^2 has the closed form:

\boxed{\quad
  \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1^2)
  \;=\; \frac{q^4 + 1}{q^2 + 1}
  \;=\; \frac{q\,[2]_{q^2}}{[2]_q}
  \;=\; 1 + \frac{q^2(q^2-1)}{q^2+1}.
\quad}

This value is independent of n, and its closure is the positive Hopf link L_+^{\mathrm{Hopf}}. At q_0 it is 1.12808874411435378559.

Because z = q^3/(q^2+1) and q - q^{-1} both lie in \mathbb{Q}(q), the trace \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1^2) is a rational function of q with no half-integral powers.

The \mathfrak{Q}_\beta factorisation takes the form:

  \mathfrak{Q}_\beta \;=\; Q_A \cdot \cos\bigl(\alpha - b\hbar_q^2/2\bigr)
              \cdot \prod_{n \geq 2} (1 + c_n \hbar_q^{2n})

with coefficients c_2 = b^2, c_3 = -2 b^3, c_4 = b^2 + 1/2. At q = 1 + \varepsilon, the \varepsilon^{2n} coefficients of \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1^2) - 1 are -1/4, -1/8, +1/16 for n = 2, 3, 4 (see Table 2), which do not match these c_n values: at n = 2 they disagree in sign, and at n = 3, 4 by an order of magnitude. Therefore, the factors 1 + c_n \hbar_q^{2n} arise from a separate categorical decomposition of \mathfrak{Q}_\beta rather than from the bare Markov trace of \sigma_1^2.

This closed form is the simplest nontrivial derived Markov trace in the framework.

Proof Proof of trm hopf sigma1 sq closed form. The Hecke quadratic relation \sigma_1^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma_1 + 1 gives \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1^2) = (q - q^{-1})\,\mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1) + \mathrm{tr}_M(1). The Markov axioms (Primitive Markov-trace axioms) fix \mathrm{tr}_M(1) = 1 and \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1) = z := q^3/(q^2+1), so

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1^2)
  \;=\; (q - q^{-1}) \cdot \frac{q^3}{q^2 + 1} + 1.

Simplifying the first term: q - q^{-1} = (q^2-1)/q, so

  (q - q^{-1})\,z
  \;=\; \frac{q^2 - 1}{q} \cdot \frac{q^3}{q^2+1}
  \;=\; \frac{q^2(q^2-1)}{q^2+1}
  \;=\; \frac{q^2\,h}{[2]_q},

writing h = q - q^{-1} and [2]_q = q + q^{-1} = (q^2+1)/q. Adding 1 over the common denominator q^2+1 gives

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1^2)
  \;=\; \frac{q^2 + 1 + q^4 - q^2}{q^2+1}
  \;=\; \frac{q^4 + 1}{q^2 + 1}
  \;=\; \frac{q\,[2]_{q^2}}{[2]_q},

using q^4 + 1 = q^2 [2]_{q^2} and q^2 + 1 = q\,[2]_q. No half-integral power of q appears; the result is rational in q.

Stabilisation (Primitive Markov-trace axioms axiom 3 and its \sigma_n^{-1} consequence) scales the trace by z for an adjoined positive crossing and by z_{-} = z - (q - q^{-1}) for a negative one. Neither case arises here: \sigma_1^2 involves only the first generator, and the Markov trace is compatible with the tower inclusions H_2(q) \subset H_n(q), so its trace in H_n for any n \geq 2 coincides with the trace in H_2 — no stabilisation factor enters because no new crossing is adjoined. ∎

Taylor expansion at q = 1 + \varepsilon

Split off the polynomial part by division:

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1^2) - 1
  \;=\; \frac{q^4 - q^2}{q^2+1}
  \;=\; q^2 - 2 + \frac{2}{q^2+1}.

Substituting q = 1 + \varepsilon, the polynomial part contributes \varepsilon^2 + 2\varepsilon - 1 and the rational part expands about a pair of conjugate poles at q = \pm i, i.e. \varepsilon = -1 \pm i:

  \bigl[\varepsilon^k\bigr]\,\frac{2}{q^2+1}
  \;=\; (-1)^k\,2^{(1-k)/2}\,
        \sin\!\Bigl(\tfrac{(k+1)\pi}{4}\Bigr),
        \qquad k \geq 0 .

So the series is a damped oscillation of period 8 in k, with radius of convergence \sqrt 2, rather than a binomial series. Its coefficients:

rem:hecke-algebra-from-braiding:
Remark The Iwahori--Hecke algebra H_n(q) as a categorical quotient. The Iwahori--Hecke algebra where normal-form computations occur is the quotient of the braid-group algebra by the minimal polynomial of the categorical braiding.

The endomorphism \sigma = \tau(c_{V,V}) satisfies the Hecke relation:

  (\sigma - q)(\sigma + q^{-1}) =  0,

where q is the braiding eigenvalue. Consequently, the Iwahori--Hecke algebra on n strands is:

  H_n(R, q) =  k[B_n] \big/
  \bigl\langle (\sigma_i - q)(\sigma_i + q^{-1})  \big| 
  i = 1, \ldots, n{-}1 \bigr\rangle.

The parameter q is a fixed categorical datum determined by the braiding. The per-crossing weights q and -q^{-1} are exactly the eigenvalues of \sigma on S^{2} V \oplus \Lambda^{2} V, forced by the categorical volume constraint.
def:f-bor-borromean-observable:
Definition Borromean categorical observable. The Borromean categorical observable is

  F_{\mathrm{Bor}}(q) \;:=\;
    \frac{\bigl|\mathrm{tr}_M(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}, q)\bigr| \cdot [3]_q!}{q^3}.

The normaliser [3]_q!/q^3 = 1 + 2q^{-2} + 2q^{-4} + q^{-6} is the Schur element c_{\mathrm{sign}} of the sign character of H_3(q), with (\sigma_i - q)(\sigma_i + q^{-1}) = 0. At the horizontal Dirac square scale q^{-2}, it equals the Poincaré polynomial of the symmetric group \mathfrak{S}_3:

  \frac{[3]_q!}{q^3}
  \;=\; (1 + q^{-2})(1 + q^{-2} + q^{-4})
  \;=\; \sum_{w \in \mathfrak{S}_3} (q^{-2})^{\ell(w)}
  \;=\; P_{\mathfrak{S}_3}(q^{-2}).

For w \in S_3 write \sigma_w for its positive braid lift in H_3(q). The Schur elements c_\chi are the constants in the decomposition \tau = \sum_\chi \chi / c_\chi of the symmetrising trace \tau(\sigma_w) = \delta_{w,1}. They are

  c_{\mathrm{triv}} = q^3\,[3]_q!, \qquad c_{\mathrm{sign}} = [3]_q!/q^3, \qquad c_{\mathrm{refl}} = [3]_q .

So F_{\mathrm{Bor}}(q) = |\mathrm{tr}_M(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}, q)| \cdot c_{\mathrm{sign}}(q). The same constant appears in x_-^2 = c_{\mathrm{sign}}\,x_- for the unnormalised q-antisymmetriser x_- = \sum_{w \in S_3} (-q)^{-\ell(w)}\,\sigma_w. The relation x_-^2 = c_{\mathrm{sign}}\,x_- is the standard quasi-idempotent identity for the sign block.

The normaliser is asserted, not derived. Every normaliser q^k [3]_q! equals |S_3| = 6 at q = 1, so the classical limit does not fix k. For q > 1, q^k [3]_q! is the Schur element of a linear character only for k = 3 (trivial) or k = -3 (sign), and it is invariant under q \mapsto q^{-1} only for k = 0. The observable uses k = -3. Two candidate algebraic routes do not produce it:

  • Let z = q^3/(q^2+1) be the Markov parameter, \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_i) = z. The Jones–Markov normalisation of a writhe-zero three-strand closure is [2]_q^2, since z \cdot \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_i^{-1}) = [2]_q^{-2}.
  • The braid word of the Borromean rings is V^3 = (\sigma_0 \sigma_1^{-1})^3. It has writhe zero and is a pure braid, so every framing correction is 1.

At z = q^3/(q^2+1), the sign block weight is y_{(1^3)} = 0, while this normaliser is that block's Schur element. That tension is open. The Markov weight of the trivial partition is y_{(3)} = (q^4+1)/(q^2+1)^2, so q^3/[3]_q! is not y_{(3)}. Relabelling the root q \mapsto -q^{-1} swaps the trivial and sign characters, and only in that relabelled frame is q^3/[3]_q! attached to the trivial partition.

A modified-trace reading of the factor q^{-3}, as a derivative in an integral, bar-invariant coordinate, is recorded with its negative result in the Kazhdan–Lusztig coordinate conjecture; it does not derive the normaliser.

Every coefficient of F_{\mathrm{Bor}} in the variable h = q - q^{-1} is an exact rational number:

  F_{\mathrm{Bor}}(h)
  \;=\; 6 \;-\; 9h \;+\; \tfrac{19}{2}h^2 \;-\; \tfrac{57}{8}h^3
        \;-\; \tfrac{1}{2}h^4 \;+\; \tfrac{649}{128}h^5 \;-\; 7h^6 \;+\; \cdots

The observable attaches two structural integers: 2 = \dim V_{(2,1)} (the dimension of the standard irreducible representation of \mathfrak{S}_3) and 12 = 2 \cdot 6 = \dim V_{(2,1)} \cdot |\mathfrak{S}_3| (the classical limit P_{\mathfrak{S}_3}(1) = |\mathfrak{S}_3| scaled by \dim V_{(2,1)}). These integers carry no archimedean information and are available over any base ring.
conj:proton-normaliser-kl-coordinate:
Conjecture The proton normaliser q^{-3} as a derivative in an integral, bar-invariant coordinate. Let x_- = \sum_{w \in S_3} (-q)^{-\ell(w)}\,\sigma_w \in H_3(q) be the sign quasi-idempotent, scaled to have coefficient 1 on the identity. Let \mathrm{tr}_z be the Markov trace with \mathrm{tr}_z(\sigma_i) = z. Then t(z) = \mathrm{tr}_z(x_-) vanishes at the Jones–Markov point z_0 = q^3/(q^2+1). Reparametrise the family by c = \mathrm{tr}_z(b) for an element b = u\,\sigma_1 + v of H_2. The conjecture states that the factor q^{-3} in the normaliser c_{\mathrm{sign}} = [3]_q!\,q^{-3} of the Borromean observable equals -\partial_c t at z_0, where b satisfies:

  1. b and 1 span H_2 over \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}], that is, u is a unit of \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}];
  2. b is fixed by the bar involution \sigma_1 \mapsto \sigma_1^{-1}, q \mapsto q^{-1}.

Stated this way, conditions (1) and (2) apply to the coordinate b only. The element x_- is fixed by its identity coefficient, which is integral but not bar-invariant. The results below show that this split carries the whole q^{-3}. So the conjecture does not derive the normaliser; it records a negative result. The normaliser of F_{\mathrm{Bor}} remains asserted.

What is proved. The elements satisfying (1) and (2) are exactly b = \pm(\sigma_1 - q) + c with c bar-invariant. For these, -\partial_c t(z_0) = u^{-1} q^{-3} with u = \pm 1, so the sign of the derivative follows the sign of u. Each condition is needed. Condition (1) alone allows u = q^m for every m \in \mathbb{Z}, which gives \pm q^{-3-m}. Condition (2) alone allows u = [2]_q, which gives q^{-3}/[2]_q. The same rule applied to the trivial quasi-idempotent x_+, whose trace vanishes at z_+ = -1/(q^3+q), gives derivative q^3. That is the q-power of the trivial Schur element c_{\mathrm{triv}} = q^3\,[3]_q!.

What weakens the conjecture. Three further results bear against it.

  • The derivative does not select the power of q. The Markov trace decomposes as \mathrm{tr}_z = y_{(3)}\chi_{\mathrm{triv}} + y_{(1^3)}\chi_{\mathrm{sign}} + y_{(2,1)}\chi_{\mathrm{refl}}. Each linear weight y has slope \pm 1/[3]_q! at its zeros. For any element x of a linear block, \mathrm{tr}_z(x) is the square constant of x (the scalar c with x^2 = c\,x) times y, so its derivative is that constant divided by [3]_q!. The value -q^{-3} is -c_{\mathrm{sign}}/[3]_q! because x_- was scaled to have coefficient 1 on the identity. The trivial-block result above follows the same way, so it is not an independent check.
  • Applied to the element too, the criterion gives k = 0. The bar involution maps x_- to q^6 x_-. So among the generators \pm q^m x_- of the integral sign line, only \pm q^3 x_- is bar-invariant. Its derivative at z_0 is -1, and its square constant is q^3 c_{\mathrm{sign}} = [3]_q!, the bar-symmetric normaliser. The conjecture holds only if the criterion applies to the coordinate but not to the element.
  • The reflection block does not follow the rule. Its weight y_{(2,1)} vanishes at z = q with slope -[2]_q^2/[3]_q!, not \pm 1/[3]_q!.

The sign line has a bar-fixed generator. Let \# be the sign twist \sigma_i \mapsto -\sigma_i^{-1} and x the q-symmetriser a_0 a_1 a_0 - a_0 with a_i = \sigma_i + q^{-1}. Then x' = \#x satisfies \sigma_i x' = -q^{-1} x', is fixed by the bar involution, and squares as x'^2 = [3]_q!\,x'. A multiple \pm q^m x' is bar-fixed only for m = 0, and the multiple with square constant c_{\mathrm{sign}} is q^{-3} x', which is not bar-fixed. So the bar-invariant Schur normaliser is [3]_q! with k = 0, and the production normaliser is q^{-3} times it. This is proved for any field, with q not a root of unity; it does not change the normaliser of F_{\mathrm{Bor}}, which remains asserted.

What is open. No axiom requires the trace family to be read in a coordinate satisfying (1) and (2). Both ingredients are defined: the bar involution, and the integral form \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}] over which traces are evaluated. The step that is not established is that the observable's normaliser is computed in such a coordinate. Deriving it would need a principle that observables factor through the integral, bar-symmetric form, which is not on record. Such a principle, applied uniformly, would select k = 0 rather than k = -3.

Conditions (1) and (2) together force u = \pm 1.
thm:borromean-word-minimal:
Theorem The Borromean word is the shortest non-trivial pure zero-linking three-braid. Let \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}} = (\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1})^3 \in B_3. Call a word in \sigma_0^{\pm 1}, \sigma_1^{\pm 1} pure zero-linking if its permutation is the identity and each of its three pairwise linking numbers is 0. Among freely reduced pure zero-linking words:

  1. every word of length at most 5 is empty;
  2. every word of length 6 is either the identity of B_3 or conjugate in B_3 to \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}};
  3. \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}} \neq 1 in B_3.

Proof

Items 1 and 2 are a finite check over all reduced words of length at most 6. At length 6 there are 16 such words. Four of them are \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}, its cyclic rotation, its mirror and the mirror's rotation; these are conjugate, because exchanging \sigma_0 \leftrightarrow \sigma_1 is conjugation by \Delta = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0. The other twelve are rotations of \Delta\,\Delta'^{-1} with \Delta' = \sigma_1\sigma_0\sigma_1, which is the identity by the braid relation. For item 3, the Burau representation at t = -1 sends \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}} to the matrix with rows (13, 8) and (8, 5).
thm:borromean-character-fibre:
Theorem Two values of the standard character determine the Borromean conjugacy class. Let \chi_{(2,1)}(q, w) be the trace of a word w in the (2,1) representation of the Hecke algebra H_3(q). Let w be a word in \sigma_0^{\pm 1}, \sigma_1^{\pm 1} of any length with writhe 0. If

  \chi_{(2,1)}(i, w) = \chi_{(2,1)}(i, \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}})
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \chi_{(2,1)}(2, w) = \chi_{(2,1)}(2, \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}),

then w is conjugate in B_3 to \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}} = (\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1})^3.

Proof

At q = i the character of a writhe-0 word equals the trace of its image under the Burau representation B_3 \to \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z}) at t = -1; for \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}} that trace is 18. Every matrix of trace greater than 2 is conjugate to a product of R = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix} and L = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}. A product with r factors R and l factors L has trace at least 2 + rl, and exactly 2 + l (or 2 + r) when only one R (or one L) occurs.

The kernel of B_3 \to \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z}) is generated by \Delta^4, which has writhe 12. Lifting the conjugacy back to B_3 therefore costs a power of \Delta^4, and writhe 0 forces r \equiv l \pmod{12}. With rl \le 16 this leaves r = l \le 4. A check over the 340 words with r = l \le 4 leaves (RL)^3, the image of \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}, and R^4L^4. The character is a class function on B_3, and R^4L^4 has a different value at q = 2.
rem:burau-invariant-form-prior-art:
Remark Prior art: the Burau representation preserves a sesquilinear form. For a matrix M over \mathbb{Z}[t, t^{-1}] let M^* be its transpose with every entry p(t) replaced by p(t^{-1}). Squier proves that there is a nonsingular (n-1) \times (n-1) matrix J_0 over \mathbb{Z}[t, t^{-1}] with \beta(w)^* J_0\, \beta(w) = J_0 for every w \in B_n, where \beta is the reduced Burau representation [squier1984, Theorem, p. 199]. Over \mathbb{Z}[s, s^{-1}] with s^2 = t, rescaling the basis by s^a turns J_0 into the Hermitian matrix

J = (s + s^{-1})\, I - \sum_a \left(e_{a-1,a} + e_{a,a+1}\right),

and each generator then acts as the reflection \beta_i(v) = v - (s^2 + 1)\, \langle e_i, v \rangle / \langle e_i, e_i \rangle \; e_i, with \langle v, w \rangle = v^* J w [squier1984, \S 3, eqs. (6)--(7), p. 201].

The proof of the Borromean fibre theorem uses the Burau representation at t = -1. There the substitution t \mapsto t^{-1} fixes t, so Squier's identity specialises to \beta(w)^{\mathsf{T}} J_0(-1)\, \beta(w) = J_0(-1): an integral bilinear form preserved by the image of B_3. The proof does not use this form; it argues from traces and the R, L normal form in \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z}).

Two points stop the form from being used at t = -1 without further work. Nonsingularity is a statement over \mathbb{Z}[t, t^{-1}], so whether J_0(-1) is still nonsingular, and what its signature is, has not been checked here. And at s = i the diagonal entry \langle e_i, e_i \rangle = s + s^{-1} is zero, so the reflection formula above is not defined at that point. The corpus's other t = -1 object, the Jordan block of the Hecke generator at q = i, is a different module, and Squier's form says nothing about it directly.
rem:borromean-word-selection:
Remark What fixes the Borromean word. The Borromean observable takes the word \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}} as input. Two results fix it.

Zero pairwise linking forces writhe 0. At writhe 0 the crossing energy of a word is its length times (q - q^{-1})/2, so for q > 1 minimising the crossing energy is minimising length. By the minimality theorem, the words of least energy among non-trivial pure zero-linking three-braids are exactly the conjugates of \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}. Minimising crossing energy therefore selects the word up to conjugacy.

The Wedderburn form of the Markov trace of a writhe-0 three-strand word depends on the word only through \chi_{(2,1)}. By the character theorem, no other conjugacy class at writhe 0, of any length, shares the value of \chi_{(2,1)} with \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}} at q = i and q = 2. So the trace seen by the mass identity does not leave room for a second word.
def:hecke-normal-form:
Definition Hecke normal form in H_n(q). The Hecke normal form of an element h \in H_n(R, q) is a representative obtained by iterated application of three rewriting rules, each oriented so that the shortlex-larger word reduces to the shortlex-smaller one:

  1. Hecke relation: \sigma_i^2 \to (q - q^{-1})\sigma_i + \mathbf{1}.
  2. Far commutativity: \sigma_i \sigma_j \to \sigma_j \sigma_i for i > j + 1.
  3. Yang--Baxter: \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \to \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i.

These three rules do not form a Gröbner--Shirshov basis, and the reduction they generate is therefore not confluent: the normal form they produce depends on the order in which rules are applied. The obstruction appears first at n = 4, where the overlap of rule 3 for (\sigma_2, \sigma_3) with rule 2 for (\sigma_3, \sigma_1) over the word \sigma_3\sigma_2\sigma_3\sigma_1 has S-polynomial \sigma_2\sigma_3\sigma_2\sigma_1 - \sigma_3\sigma_2\sigma_1\sigma_3, in which both words are already irreducible.

Confluence is recovered by completing the system with the Bokut--Shiao family [bokut2001]

\sigma_i \sigma_{i-1} \cdots \sigma_j \sigma_i \;\to\; \sigma_{i-1} \sigma_i \sigma_{i-1} \cdots \sigma_j
\qquad (j \leq i - 1),

which subsumes rule 3 at j = i - 1 and which carries no q: it is a braid-group identity, obtained by commuting \sigma_i past \sigma_{i-2} \cdots \sigma_j and then applying the braid relation, with the quadratic relation never used. The refuting S-polynomial above is, up to sign, exactly this rule at (i, j) = (3, 1); for the completed system it is therefore no longer a normal form, and the n = 4 obstruction is gone (compare the analogous completion on the Temperley--Lieb quotient in [kimlee2018]).

The completed system is a Gröbner--Shirshov basis for every n \geq 1 and every admissible q-datum, and its normal forms are consequently unique by the Diamond Lemma of George M. Bergman [bergman1978], which applies directly over any commutative base ring R (in particular R = \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}]) once leading coefficients are units, continuing the constructive finite-step ideal-membership and composition-lemma tradition initiated for commutative polynomial ideals by Grete Hermann [hermann1926] and for nonassociative and associative algebras by Anatoly I. Shirshov [shirshov1962]. Standard monomials for the completed system index an R-free basis of H_n(R, q) of rank n!, in bijection with the symmetric group S_n [dipper-james1986]. Computationally, the reduction may be evaluated by directed Kashiwara crystal traversal rather than by S-polynomial overlap analysis.
rem:markov-moves-brane-tower:
Remark Markov moves as horizontal and vertical components. The two Markov moves that ensure link invariance correspond to the horizontal and vertical directions of the brane tower's cosimplicial structure.

Conjugation \beta \mapsto \gamma\beta\gamma^{-1} is the horizontal direction. It represents gauge transformations within a single fibre at a fixed level n. The trace property \mathrm{tr}_M(ab) = \mathrm{tr}_M(ba) guarantees invariance under these moves.

Stabilisation \beta \mapsto \beta \cdot \sigma_n^{\pm 1} is the vertical direction. It represents movement between levels of the tower via jet prolongation A_n \hookrightarrow A_{n+1}. The Markov property — \mathrm{tr}_M(x \sigma_n) = z\,\mathrm{tr}_M(x) for a positive crossing, \mathrm{tr}_M(x \sigma_n^{-1}) = z_{-}\,\mathrm{tr}_M(x) with z_{-} = z - (q - q^{-1}) for a negative one (Markov axioms) — correctly scales the trace across these inclusions.

Thus, the Iwahori--Hecke algebra tower shadows the brane tower. Markov's theorem dictates that horizontal and vertical moves exhaust the gauge freedom. The direct limit algebra \mathcal{A}_\infty = \varinjlim\mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A_n) provides the receptacle where the Markov trace stabilises to a well-defined link invariant.
def:polygonal-link-type:
Definition Polygonal links and link types. A polygonal link in a real inner-product space V is a finite family of closed polygons in V whose carriers are simple and pairwise disjoint.

A \Delta-move replaces one edge [a,b] of a component by the two edges [a,c] and [c,b], or performs the inverse replacement, provided the triangle with vertices a, b, c meets the link only in the edge [a,b]. Re-indexing the components and re-indexing the vertices of a component are also \Delta-moves.

Two polygonal links are \Delta-equivalent when a finite sequence of \Delta-moves carries one to the other. The link type of a polygonal link is its \Delta-equivalence class. Throughout this paper, "link type" and "isotopic link" refer to this class. For \dim V = 3 the class coincides with the PL ambient isotopy class (Reidemeister; see Lickorish, Chapter 1).
rem:topological-vs-pl-link-type:
Remark Topological links and polygonal link types. A topological link enters this paper only through a polygonal representative, and such links are tame. The link type of a polygonal link is a PL notion. Its relation to topological ambient isotopy has two parts.

  1. Smooth isotopies. If two polygonal links are joined by a C^1 ambient isotopy, they have the same link type. Sampling each component finely enough keeps the inscribed polygons simple and disjoint along the isotopy, yielding a sequence of elementary \Delta-moves.

  2. Topological isotopies. A topological ambient isotopy cannot in general be replaced by a C^1 one, because a C^1 diffeomorphism cannot carry the carrier of a triangle onto the carrier of a square. In dimension three, topologically ambient isotopic tame links are PL ambient isotopic. This follows from Moise's triangulation theorem and Bing's tameness theorem [moise1952, bing1954]. Here this comparison is cited from the three-manifold literature rather than proved from scratch, so equality of link types for topologically isotopic links is conditional on the Moise–Bing theorem.

  3. The ambient space. The definition is stated in a real inner-product space V, while the Alexander--Markov remarks place links in S^3. For \dim V = 3 the two settings give the same link types. A compact link in S^3 = \mathbb{R}^3 \cup \{\infty\} misses a point, and an ambient isotopy of S^3 can be adjusted to fix a point off the link, so the classification of tame links up to ambient isotopy is the same in \mathbb{R}^3 and in S^3 [rolfsen, lickorish1997]. The cited Moise--Bing comparison likewise concerns \dim V = 3; only the three-dimensional case is supported by the classical triangulation theorems.

The link type defined here is distinct from the two-element type of braid link types, which enumerates only the unknot and the Hopf link.
rem:markov-trace-ambient-s3:
Remark The ambient three-sphere S^3 is the target of the Alexander--Markov correspondence: \mathrm{tr}_M is by construction a link invariant in S^3. The ambient three-sphere S^3 enters strictly through the closure construction via two classical theorems.

Alexander's theorem states that every oriented link in S^3 is the closure of some braid. Therefore, the disjoint union of braid groups exhausts all link types in the three-sphere.

Markov's theorem establishes that two braids have closures of the same link type in S^3, that is, PL ambient isotopic closures, if and only if they are related by a sequence of conjugation and stabilisation moves.

The Markov trace is invariant under both moves. Because closure surjects onto the links of S^3 and its fibres are exactly the Markov-move orbits, the Markov trace descends to a well-defined invariant of links in S^3. The ambient S^3 is thus constructed categorically as the target of the Alexander--Markov correspondence, rather than posited geometrically upstream.

The closure construction fixes this ambient S^3 independently of the gauge group, which enters only through the representation category. Whether the coincidence \mathrm{SU}(2) \cong S^3 is structural or incidental here remains open.
prop:closure-unseen-subword:
Proposition No closure distinguishes two elements exactly when they differ by a commutator; closure is a Bell pairing. Let R be a commutative ring and A an R-algebra. Call an R-linear map t : A \to M a trace if t(xy) = t(yx) for all x, y \in A, and let [A, A] be the R-span of all xy - yx.

  1. For a, b \in A, every trace satisfies t(a) = t(b) if and only if a - b \in [A, A]. The quotient map A \to A/[A, A] = \mathrm{HH}_0(A) is the universal trace.

  2. For a unit u \in A and any w \in A, every trace satisfies t(u w u^{-1}) = t(w).

  3. Let \Omega = \sum_i e_i \otimes e_i \in R^n \otimes R^n. For every X \in M_n(R),

      (X \otimes 1)\,\Omega = (1 \otimes X^{\mathsf T})\,\Omega,
  \qquad
  \langle \Omega, (X \otimes 1)\,\Omega \rangle = \mathrm{tr}\,X .

Proof. (1) A trace vanishes on each generator xy - yx of [A, A], so by linearity it vanishes on [A, A]; this gives the reverse direction. The quotient map A \to A/[A, A] is itself a trace, because xy - yx \in [A, A]. Applying the hypothesis to it gives a - b \in [A, A]. (2) u w u^{-1} - w = (uw)u^{-1} - u^{-1}(uw) is a commutator, so (1) applies. (3) Both sides of the first identity have (i, j) entry X_{ij}, and \langle \Omega, (X \otimes 1)\Omega \rangle = \sum_i X_{ii}. \square

In the braid setting, A = H_n(q) and the closure of a braid word is a trace on A (Markov trace). Item (1) says what a closure cannot see. The relation a \sim b \iff a - b \in [A, A] is exactly the fibre of the map to Hochschild homology \mathrm{HH}_0. Item (3) is the form closure takes on a matrix algebra: the coevaluation prepares \Omega, the evaluation projects onto it.
rem:braid-closure-physical-reading:
Remark Braid closure adds cups and caps, not crossings: two steps, and what an unseen intermediate is. Closing a braid adds a coevaluation (cup) below each strand and an evaluation (cap) above it. It adds no crossing. An observation in this framework inserts a crossing, so closure is not an observation.

Cups and caps as entangled pairs. The coevaluation of V is the maximally entangled vector \Omega of the proposition, item 3. With the pivotal weight K = \mathrm{diag}(q, q^{-1}) on V = R^2 it becomes the q-weighted vector \Omega_K, and the quantum trace of a braid \beta on V^{\otimes n} is \langle \Omega_K, (\beta \otimes 1)\,\Omega_K \rangle. Read: the cups prepare n entangled pairs, \beta acts on one half of each pair, and the caps project back onto the pairs. Each return arc is the entangled partner of its strand.

Two steps. The word closure covers two different maps.

  1. Annular closure keeps the closure axis. It is the map H_n(q) \to \mathrm{HH}_0(H_n(q)) of item 1 of the proposition, and it keeps every character \chi_\lambda separately.
  2. Forgetting the axis sends each block to its quantum dimension. The result is the Markov trace at z = q^3/(q^2+1), which averages the blocks.

What an unseen intermediate is. A process that emits u, runs w, and reabsorbs u^{-1} has the same value as w under every closure (item 2): u passes round the return arc and cancels. More generally, a subword is invisible to every closure exactly when removing it changes the element by a commutator (item 1). This gives a precise meaning to an intermediate that is produced and not seen, without a virtual particle.

Fluid dynamics. The helicity of a vortex tangle is a closure invariant. Its classical counterpart is the asymptotic linking number, in which long orbit segments are closed by short paths whose contribution vanishes in the limit [komendarczyk2008]; the closing arcs are again unseen.

Which physical object the closure axis is (a photon loop, a periodic direction, or nothing) is an interpretation and is not derived here.
prop:aether-massive-regime:
Proposition The Temperley--Lieb anisotropy \Delta = \tfrac{1}{2}(q + q^{-1}) exceeds unity for every real q \neq 1. Let q \in \mathbb{R} with q > 0 and q \neq 1, and set

  \delta(q) = q + q^{-1}, \qquad \Delta(q) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\delta(q).

Then \Delta(q) > 1.

Here \delta is the Temperley--Lieb loop weight, the balanced quantum integer [2]_q, and \Delta is the anisotropy of the associated spin chain. The proof is the arithmetic--geometric mean inequality in the form q + q^{-1} - 2 = (q-1)^2/q, which is strictly positive exactly when q \neq 1.

Two features of the statement matter more than its difficulty.

First, the hypothesis is only q \neq 1. No calibration input enters, and no parameter is available to adjust: the conclusion is forced by the aether being a genuine deformation rather than the classical point. Writing q = e^{\lambda} gives \Delta = \cosh \lambda, so the inequality is the statement that a real deformation parameter cannot produce |\Delta| < 1.

Second, the value \Delta = 1 is a phase boundary rather than an arbitrary threshold. The regime \Delta > 1 is the massive, Ising-like phase of the chain; the regime |\Delta| < 1 is the massless phase, reached only on |q| = 1. The contrapositive is recorded alongside the proposition: an anisotropy at or below unity forces q = 1, so the massless phase is unreachable from a real aether parameter.

Algebraic structure

The algebraic content is stated over a generic field, with no ordering and no archimedean construct, and the inequality is separated into its own section over \mathbb{R}. Two scalar identities are recorded as well:

  2\Delta(q) + h(q) = 2q, \qquad 2\Delta(q) - h(q) = 2q^{-1},
  \qquad h(q) = q - q^{-1},

which say that the anisotropy and the Hecke parameter recombine to q and q^{-1}. These are the entries in which the Temperley--Lieb generator differs from an undeformed exchange operator, and they are what the identification in the accompanying remark rests on.
rem:tl-is-the-xxz-chain:
Remark The production trace computes in the algebra of a one-dimensional spin chain. The production Markov trace is the \mathrm{SU}_q(2) / Temperley--Lieb one: a fibre of quantum dimension [N]_q forces the Ocneanu parameter to satisfy z\,[N]_q = q^{N}, and at N = 2 this is the convention in use. What that fixes is an algebra; the present remark records what that algebra is as a mechanics.

Let e_i denote the Temperley--Lieb generator acting on neighbouring tensor factors of V^{\otimes n}, with V the two-dimensional fibre. Then

  -2\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} e_i
  \;=\;
  H_{\mathrm{XXZ}}
  \;-\; \Delta\,(n-1)\,\mathbb{I}
  \;-\; \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(q - q^{-1}\bigr)\bigl(\sigma^z_1 - \sigma^z_n\bigr),

where H_{\mathrm{XXZ}} = \sum_i \bigl(\sigma^x_i \sigma^x_{i+1} + \sigma^y_i \sigma^y_{i+1} + \Delta\,\sigma^z_i \sigma^z_{i+1}\bigr) and \Delta is the anisotropy of the accompanying proposition. The right-hand side is the open U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)-symmetric chain on n sites: the surface term proportional to q - q^{-1} is what replaces the \mathrm{SU}(2) symmetry of the isotropic chain by its quantum deformation, and it is a boundary term because the per-bond contributions telescope.

The identification is not an additional hypothesis. It follows from the two scalar identities recorded in the proposition, which are exactly the entries of the two-site operator in the singlet channel; the remaining entries are identically zero on both sides.

Consequences

Three follow without further input.

The chain is gapped. Since \Delta > 1 for every real q \neq 1, the chain sits in the massive regime. Bound states of several down spins --- Bethe strings --- are stable there, whereas in the massless regime they are not.

The gap is small. The relevant elliptic scale is \exp\bigl(-\pi^2 / 2\log q\bigr), which at the aether is of order 10^{-21}. The chain is therefore only marginally inside the massive phase, and any statement about its spectrum that is not uniform in \Delta - 1 should be treated as delicate.

Bound states in one dimension need not be pairwise. In the exactly soluble attractive case, an n-particle string binds as n(n^2-1) rather than as the \binom{n}{2} of a pairwise sum, an enhancement of (n+1)/3 over pairwise additivity. This is the shape of object the many-body binding term elsewhere in the framework is missing, and it is available here in closed form.

Scope

The matrix identity above is verified numerically at both documented aether anchors, to the precision of the computation, and is not proved; what is proved are the scalar identities on which it rests, not the assembly.

Nothing here identifies the sites of the chain with any physical object. The claim is about the algebra the trace computes in, not about what it is a chain of.
